name: Software as a Medical Device
title: Software as a Medical Device
answer: Software as a Medical Device covers software that is itself a medical device, meaning it is intended for a medical purpose and performs its function without relying on a hardware medical device to achieve that purpose. It includes products that diagnose, prevent, monitor, treat, or alleviate disease, such as triage tools, image analysis aids, dose calculators, and digital therapeutics. The category also covers AI and machine learning models that output clinical predictions or recommendations, whether they run on a phone, a workstation, or in the cloud. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and many of them sit in or near this regulatory category. The boundary matters because a general wellness app or an administrative tool is not SaMD, while a tool that informs clinical decisions usually is.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future
Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security

sections.body: Software as a Medical Device covers software that is itself a medical device, meaning it is intended for a medical purpose and performs its function without relying on a hardware medical device to achieve that purpose. It includes products that diagnose, prevent, monitor, treat, or alleviate disease, such as triage tools, image analysis aids, dose calculators, and digital therapeutics. The category also covers AI and machine learning models that output clinical predictions or recommendations, whether they run on a phone, a workstation, or in the cloud. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and many of them sit in or near this regulatory category. The boundary matters because a general wellness app or an administrative tool is not SaMD, while a tool that informs clinical decisions usually is.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: SaMD runs on general purpose computing platforms, including smartphones, tablets, browsers, clinical workstations, on premise servers, and cloud services. The runtime stack typically includes a model or algorithm, an application layer, data storage, interfaces to electronic health records, and monitoring and logging components. Because the software is the device, the platform, operating system, dependencies, and update mechanism are part of the regulated product. Security controls such as encryption, access management, audit trails, and secure update channels are therefore part of the infrastructure, not optional add-ons. Some SaMD is deployed at the edge for low latency, while other products rely on centralized cloud inference and periodic model updates.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work on SaMD follows a controlled software lifecycle, with requirements, design, verification, validation, risk management, and clinical evaluation documented in a quality management system. Teams classify the product by risk and intended use, then assemble evidence that the software performs as intended and that residual risks are acceptable. For AI enabled products, that evidence often includes training data description, performance testing, subgroup analysis, human factors review, and a plan for managing model changes over time. Post market surveillance, complaint handling, and cybersecurity monitoring continue after release. Changes are managed through formal change control, and some regulators allow a predetermined change control plan for anticipated model updates.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance for SaMD covers data rights, patient privacy, intellectual property, model provenance, and liability. Manufacturers need clear rights to training and validation data, documented data lineage, and controls over how patient data is used and shared. Provenance records, model cards, and audit trails help regulators, clinicians, and buyers understand what a model was trained on and how it has changed. The site tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages and 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows how quickly governance questions can become legal disputes. Cybersecurity risk is also a patient safety risk, so incident response, vulnerability management, and coordinated disclosure are part of the governance picture.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more continuous oversight of AI enabled SaMD, with regulators, health systems, and manufacturers working on ways to review and update models without starting from zero each time. Expect more emphasis on real world performance monitoring, drift detection, transparency, and post market evidence. International harmonization and reliance arrangements may reduce duplicate reviews, though local requirements will remain. Security and supply chain scrutiny will likely grow as more devices depend on cloud services and third party components. The field is also moving toward clearer methods for documenting data provenance and for assigning responsibility when a model contributes to harm.
